lesson_title: The Shortcut That Fails: Compound and Double Angles
hook_text: Sine of 90 is 1. Sine 60 plus sine 30 is 1,37. The most tempting shortcut in trigonometry is off by a third — here is what actually works.
clip_script: Everyone wants sine of 60 plus 30 to be sine 60 plus sine 30. Test it. Sine of 90 is exactly 1. Sine 60 plus sine 30? About 1,37. The shortcut overshoots by a third, because angles combine by rotation — the second tilt starts from an already-tilted ramp, so part of its effort goes sideways. The real recipe blends both angles: sine alpha cos beta plus cos alpha sine beta. And check it: sine 30 cos 60 is a quarter, cos 30 sine 60 is three quarters — total, exactly 1. The recipe even builds angles the calculator table never had: fifteen degrees is 45 minus 30, and cosine of it comes out as root 6 plus root 2, over 4 — exact, no decimals. Then fold the recipe onto itself, beta equals alpha, and the double angles drop out free: sine 2 alpha is 2 sine alpha cos alpha, and cos 2 alpha wears three different costumes for three different jobs. One failed shortcut, one blending recipe, one fold. That is the whole topic.
visual_style: A skate ramp tilting in two stages against a sunset sky, angle arcs glowing on each tilt, surd fractions assembling like puzzle pieces into root 6 plus root 2 over 4, then a paper identity folding in half.
mood: Myth-busting, kinetic, a satisfying click when the quarter and three quarters sum to one.
pacing: A fast wrong answer, a hard brake on the 1,37, then smooth confident assembly of the true recipe.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never lose the compound-angle marks again.
